paras: The assault on Frank Holland and Nelson Peters was an attack by striking teamsters on two Black non-union coal drivers at Chestnut and Point streets in Providence, Rhode Island, on the morning of April 18, 1903. After both were beaten and stoned, Holland fired into the crowd and wounded the striker Edward Baxter; a second striker, William O'Neil, was hurt when the discarded revolver went off. The Providence News put the shooting on its front page, and wire reports carried it to New York, Portland, Maine, and Manchester, New Hampshire.

The shooting grew out of a teamsters' strike: according to a wire account, about forty men formerly employed by the Eastern Coal Company were not taken back when the dispute was settled, and the company kept their replacements. The union turned its efforts against that company, and during the week drivers were stoned and beaten and loads of coal dumped in the streets.

Holland, of 40 Wade Street, and Peters, both described as "colored," were on their way to work at about 6:30 a.m. when a group of about ten men, said to be locked-out union drivers, accosted them. According to the Providence News, Baxter asked Holland where he could get a job while another man attacked Holland from behind. Holland was knocked down and kicked, Peters was beaten against a fence, and stones struck Holland in the face and head. Holland later said the crowd called him a "black —" and that he heard cries of "kill them," including from men who came out of a nearby saloon.

Holland then drew a .22-calibre revolver and fired five shots into the crowd, hitting Baxter twice, before throwing the weapon away and escaping with Peters. In the police version carried by the wire, Howland warned that he would shoot before aiming, the crowd scattered, and the shots "probably saved them from being mobbed." Taken into a barroom at South and Richmond streets, the revolver went off again and wounded William O'Neil in the side. O'Neil went to the Rhode Island Hospital, and Police Surgeon Griffin cut a bullet from Baxter's neck at the Fifth station.

Holland went to work after the attack but returned home when his face pained him, and Lieutenant Gilmartan arrested him there at about 10 o'clock. The Providence News reported that Baxter was held for an assault upon Holland and that O'Neil, still in the hospital, was under surveillance for an assault upon Peters. The wire account instead said Baxter was arrested on a charge of obstructing the property of the Eastern Coal Company. Two other strikers were fined that day for attacks on teamsters, and twenty officers were sent to the coal yards. No report of a later hearing or trial for Holland, Baxter or O'Neil appears in the coverage.

The Providence News ran the story on its front page the same day under the headline "Union Teamster Baxter Shot by Non Union Driver" and called it "a very serious labor disturbance." Its longer account, however, detailed the attack on the two drivers, the only people it identified by race, and printed Holland's statement about the slur and the cries to kill them.

Outside Rhode Island the story ran as a short wire item, first in the Alexandria Gazette's "Telegraphic Brevities" that same day. The New-York Tribune headed it "Striker at Providence Shot" and repeated an allegation that Baxter had held up Howland's horses. The Portland Daily Press ("Used Revolver on Mob") and the New Hampshire Farmer and Weekly Union ("Howland Fires into Crowd") instead cast the driver as defending himself. No Black newspaper account was found; all known reports appeared in white papers.

The papers disagreed on the driver's name, with the Providence News and the Alexandria Gazette using Holland and the other wire versions Howland. The local paper and the police version had the two men on foot going to work, while the Alexandria and New York briefs had them delivering coal. The Alexandria Gazette said Holland had not yet been arrested and both strikers were seriously wounded; the Providence News reported his arrest and called neither of Baxter's wounds dangerous.

accounts.label: Providence News local report
accounts.gist: Ten men accosted the two drivers on foot on their way to work; Baxter distracted Holland while another struck him from behind; both were beaten and stoned before Holland fired.

accounts.label: Frank Holland's statement
accounts.gist: The crowd called him a 'black —' and he heard cries of 'kill them' from the crowd and from men coming out of a nearby saloon.

accounts.label: Police version (wire)
accounts.gist: Baxter and others attacked Howland and Peters while they were going to work and struck them repeatedly with stones; Howland warned he would shoot and aimed the pistol, and the crowd scattered.

accounts.label: Wire report (delivery version)
accounts.gist: The men were attempting to deliver coal when strikers approached to drive them from the wagon; the Tribune added an allegation that Baxter had held up Howland's horses.

framing.detail: The Providence News headlined 'Union Teamster Baxter Shot by Non Union Driver' and called it 'a very serious labor disturbance', but its full account detailed the attack on the drivers and printed Holland's statement.
The Alexandria Gazette and New-York Tribune ran wire briefs ('Striker at Providence Shot') centered on the striker's wounding, the Tribune adding the claim that Baxter had held up Howland's horses.
The Portland Daily Press ('Used Revolver on Mob') and New Hampshire Farmer ('Howland Fires into Crowd') framed the driver as defending himself against a crowd that had attacked him.

conflicts.note: The local paper and the Alexandria wire brief use Holland; other wire versions use Howland.

info: April 18, 1903, about 6:30 a.m. (Portland Daily Press says 'this afternoon')
Corner of Chestnut and Point streets (Chestnut near Point), Providence
Frank Holland (spelled Howland in wire reports), of 40 Wade street, and Nelson Peters, both described as colored non-union drivers for the Eastern Coal Company
No crime was alleged against the drivers before the attack; they had taken places of strikers. The Tribune alleged Howland's horses had been held up by Baxter.
Striking or locked-out union coal teamsters, including Edward Baxter; William O'Neil was held for an assault on Peters
